title: C1465 — LH front impact severity sensor connector
introduction:
Use this reference to connect the left-hand front impact severity sensor’s identity with its connector drawing, circuit assignments and pigtail listing. I start with CNumber and Description, then check the harness association. The housing outline helps you navigate, but the circuit identifiers do the precise work—rather like reading a luggage tag instead of trusting the suitcase’s shape.

Follow a cavity label from the drawing into the Cavity column, then read across the same row. Circuit Number identifies the circuit, Color records its printed color code, and Function describes the connection’s stated role. The sensor and control-module descriptions belong to their respective rows. Keep their full wording, including the trailing dash, without treating that dash as an established polarity marking.

This is an identification and reading guide. It does not teach physical access, restraint-system preparation, disconnection, probing, testing or replacement. Physical viewing direction, gauge convention and the meanings of Box, Size and Used are unspecified here; those entries remain reference data rather than dimensions, wire-selection guidance or test criteria.

edits.why: The illustration places the vertically arranged cavity labels inside a rounded area, with a rectangular feature to its left. I use those visible landmarks to stay oriented on the page and connect each cavity label with its table row. They do not establish which side of a physical connector should face the reader.

Read each row as a complete description: cavity, circuit identifier, color code, gauge entry, function and terminal reference stay together. That preserves the distinction between the sensor and control-module connections. Their names describe the map; they do not supply expected voltage, resistance or a fault conclusion. The empty Qualifier cells add no further applicability condition.

The pigtail listing ties its Number and Service Part fields to an Engineering Shell reference, alongside the other catalog attributes. I distinguish that service assembly from the terminal reference in the circuit table and the housing identity in the connector information. This keeps the parts lookup from becoming a game of ordering whichever identifier looks most official. It provides reference relationships, not a reason to replace anything or instructions for doing so.
